question:
Choose the idiom/phrase that can substitute the underlined group of words meaningfully.

All my efforts to control the matter failed miserably.
(AOS Finance)
options: Go down the drain
Nook and cranny
Smash hit
Crack a book
solution:
The correct answer is: Go down the drain

Explanation:
The phrase "go down the drain" means to be wasted or lost, often referring to efforts, money, or plans that fail completely. In this context, the speaker's efforts to control the matter failed miserably, making this idiom the best fit.

Let's Explain All IDIOMS & Their Meanings:

[Go down the drain] – बेकार चला जाना / नष्ट हो जाना – To be wasted or ruined.
Example: "All his savings went down the drain after his business failed."

[Nook and cranny] – हर छोटी-बड़ी जगह – Every small or hidden part of a place.
Example: "She searched every nook and cranny of the house but couldn’t find her keys."

[Smash hit] – बहुत बड़ी सफलता – A huge success (usually in entertainment).
Example: "The new movie became a smash hit worldwide."

[Crack a book] – किताब खोलकर पढ़ना – To open a book and study (often used negatively).
Example: "He never cracks a book but still scores well in exams."

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Go down the drain" is "to be wasted or fail completely" because it perfectly describes the situation where all efforts to control the matter were unsuccessful. The other options do not fit the context of failure or wasted effort.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
One’s gut feeling
(Assistant)
options: An illogical emotion
A burden
A factual opinion
An instinct or intuition
solution:
The correct answer is: An instinct or intuition

Explanation:
"One’s gut feeling" - "अपनी अंतर्दृष्टि या सहज बोध"
The idiom refers to an immediate, instinctive reaction or understanding of a situation, often without conscious reasoning.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the idea that gut (stomach) sensations are linked to emotional responses. Historically, people believed intuition came from the gut, leading to expressions like "gut instinct."

Example:
"She had a gut feeling that something was wrong, so she decided not to take the job."
"उसे एक सहज बोध हुआ कि कुछ गड़बड़ है, इसलिए उसने नौकरी लेने से मना कर दिया।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "One’s gut feeling" is "An instinct or intuition" because it describes an innate sense rather than a logical or emotional response. The other options do not align with the idiom's true meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
The best thing since sliced bread
(Constable GD Examination 2022)
options: An openly performed confession
A sincerely made apology
A really good invention
A thoroughly examined food
solution:
The correct answer is: A really good invention

Explanation:
"The best thing since sliced bread" - "एक बहुत ही अच्छा आविष्कार"
This idiom is used to describe something that is considered extremely useful, innovative, or excellent. Sliced bread itself was a revolutionary convenience when it was first introduced, so anything called "the best thing since sliced bread" is being praised as a significant improvement or breakthrough.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originated in the early 20th century when pre-sliced bread was introduced as a major convenience in households. It became a benchmark for innovation, leading people to compare new inventions or ideas favorably to sliced bread.

Example:
"This new smartphone is the best thing since sliced bread!"
"यह नया स्मार्टफोन बेहद उपयोगी आविष्कार है!"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "The best thing since sliced bread" is "A really good invention" because it highlights something highly innovative or beneficial. The other options—confession, apology, or food examination—do not relate to the idiom's meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Chill out
(Stenographer 2020)
options: Become stiff
Eat spicy food
Feel very cold
Relax completely
solution:
The correct answer is: Relax completely

Explanation:
"Chill out" - "पूरी तरह आराम करना"
The idiom "chill out" means to relax or calm down, often used informally to tell someone to stop being stressed or agitated.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originated in American slang in the 1970s, derived from the word "chill," meaning to cool down or relax. Over time, "chill out" became a common way to encourage someone to take it easy.

Example:
"After a long day at work, I just want to chill out and watch TV."
"काम के लंबे दिन के बाद, मैं बस टीवी देखकर आराम करना चाहता हूँ।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "chill out" is "Relax completely" because it directly conveys the idea of unwinding and reducing stress. The other options ("Become stiff," "Eat spicy food," "Feel very cold") are unrelated to the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Backseat driver
(CHSL Exam 2022 Tier I)
options: To miss an appointed meeting.
Attempt to get control over someone.
To conclude proceedings.
A person who offers unsolicited advice.
solution:
The correct answer is: A person who offers unsolicited advice.

Explanation:
"Backseat driver" - "बिना माँगे सलाह देने वाला व्यक्ति"
This idiom refers to someone who gives unwanted advice or tries to control a situation from a position where they have no authority, much like a passenger in the backseat of a car who constantly tells the driver how to drive.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the literal scenario where a passenger in the backseat of a car keeps giving unnecessary instructions to the driver, despite not being in control of the vehicle. Over time, it evolved into a metaphor for anyone who interferes without being asked.

Example:
"Even though I know how to cook, my mother-in-law keeps telling me what to do—she's such a backseat driver!"
"भले ही मुझे खाना बनाना आता है, मेरी सास मुझे बताती रहती है कि क्या करना चाहिए—वह एकदम बिना माँगे सलाह देने वाली है!"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "backseat driver" is "a person who offers unsolicited advice" because it perfectly describes someone who interferes without being asked. The other options are unrelated to this idiom's meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To read between the lines
(Paper II English Language and Comprehension)
options: To criticise the writer’s style
To read each line carefully
To interrupt someone while reading
To understand the implied meaning
solution:
The correct answer is: To understand the implied meaning

Explanation:
"To read between the lines" - "छिपे हुए अर्थ को समझना"
This idiom means to grasp the hidden or implied meaning behind what is explicitly stated, rather than taking words at face value.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from the practice of deciphering coded or hidden messages in written text, where the true meaning was not directly stated but could be inferred by carefully analyzing the content.

Example:
"When she said she was 'fine,' I could tell she was upset—I had to read between the lines."
"जब उसने कहा कि वह 'ठीक है,' मैं समझ गया कि वह परेशान थी—मुझे छिपे अर्थ को समझना पड़ा।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "To read between the lines" is "To understand the implied meaning" because it refers to interpreting the deeper or unspoken message in communication. The other options do not relate to this figurative meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
It is wise to sit on the fence and not become a party to another World War.
(SICPO Paper I 2022)
options: A person's lack of decisiveness, neutrality or hesitance to choose between two sides in an argument or a competition
Defending the no man’s land
Become a peacemaker between two fighting or competing parties.
Overtaking the thing of interest that the other parties are fighting for while they are fighting
solution:
The correct answer is: A person's lack of decisiveness, neutrality or hesitance to choose between two sides in an argument or a competition

Explanation:
"Sit on the fence" - "दोनों पक्षों के बीच निर्णय न लेना या तटस्थ रहना"
The idiom implies avoiding commitment to either side in a dispute or conflict, maintaining neutrality instead of taking a stand.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the literal image of someone sitting on a fence, neither on one side nor the other, symbolizing indecision or unwillingness to take a position.

Example:
"Politicians often sit on the fence during controversial debates to avoid alienating voters."
"राजनेता अक्सर विवादास्पद बहसों के दौरान मतदाताओं को नाराज़ न करने के लिए तटस्थ रहते हैं।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "sit on the fence" is "A person's lack of decisiveness, neutrality or hesitance to choose between two sides in an argument or a competition" because it reflects the idea of avoiding commitment to either side. The other options describe unrelated scenarios, such as defending territory, mediating, or exploiting conflicts.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.The tail wagging the dog.
(Warden Superintendent)
options: A funny and unexpected situation where the opposite of an expected outcome happens
A situation where a powerful person is being controlled by someone less powerful
A strange and bizarre incident that defies normal everyday logic
A difficult situation that baffles people but it is by no means implausible
solution:
The correct answer is: A situation where a powerful person is being controlled by someone less powerful

Explanation:
"The tail wagging the dog" - "कमजोर व्यक्ति द्वारा शक्तिशाली व्यक्ति पर नियंत्रण"
This idiom describes a scenario where a less important or weaker entity (the tail) exerts control over a more dominant one (the dog), reversing the expected power dynamic.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the literal image of a dog's tail wagging, which is normally controlled by the dog. If the tail were to wag the dog instead, it would imply an unnatural reversal of roles. The idiom gained popularity in political and organizational contexts to describe situations where subordinates or minor elements dictate major decisions.

Example:
"In that company, the junior employees make all the decisions—it's a classic case of the tail wagging the dog."
"उस कंपनी में जूनियर कर्मचारी ही सभी फैसले लेते हैं—यह 'कमजोर द्वारा शक्तिशाली पर नियंत्रण' का उदाहरण है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "The tail wagging the dog" is "A situation where a powerful person is being controlled by someone less powerful" because it captures the essence of an inverted power hierarchy. The other options describe unrelated scenarios and do not align with the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.Bite someone’s head off
(Constable GD 2021)
options: Ask someone the same question again and again
Speak angrily without any reason
Scold someone for misbehaving
Go on repeating the same point
solution:
The correct answer is: Speak angrily without any reason

Explanation:
"Bite someone’s head off" - "बिना किसी कारण के गुस्से में बोलना"
This idiom means to respond to someone in an extremely angry or aggressive manner, often without any justifiable reason. It implies an overreaction to a situation.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from the imagery of an animal (like a predator) violently attacking its prey by biting its head off. Over time, it evolved into a metaphorical expression describing harsh, unwarranted verbal outbursts.

Example:
"When I asked if he had finished the report, he bit my head off for no reason!"
"जब मैंने पूछा कि क्या उसने रिपोर्ट पूरी कर ली, तो उसने बिना किसी वजह मुझ पर गुस्सा निकाल दिया!"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Bite someone’s head off" is "Speak angrily without any reason" because it conveys an unjustified angry reaction. The other options describe repetitive questioning or scolding, which do not match the idiom's meaning.

question:
Choose the most appropriate meaning of the below quoted idiom from the below options:

“Once in a blue moon”
(Forest Guard)
options: rarely
never
frequently
regularly
solution:
The correct answer is: rarely

Explanation:
"Once in a blue moon" - "बहुत कम, नाममात्र को"
This idiom means something that happens very infrequently or almost never. The phrase "blue moon" refers to an uncommon event—a second full moon in a single calendar month—which happens roughly every 2-3 years. Hence, the idiom signifies rarity.

Origin of the Idiom:
The term "blue moon" originally referred to an extra full moon in a season (three instead of the usual two). Over time, its meaning shifted to the second full moon in a month. The idiom "once in a blue moon" emerged from this rare astronomical occurrence to describe something that happens very seldom.

Example:
"He visits his hometown once in a blue moon."
"वह अपने गाँव बहुत कम ही जाता है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "once in a blue moon" is "rarely" because it describes an event that occurs extremely infrequently. The other options ("never," "frequently," "regularly") do not match the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom that best explains the given sentence.
I was unable to solve the geometry question myself. So, I have asked my teacher to help me out.
(CHSL 2023 Tier II Extra Time)
options: Two wrongs don’t make a right.
You can’t always get what you want.
When the going gets tough, the tough gets going.
Two heads are better than one.
solution:
The correct answer is: Two heads are better than one.

Explanation:
The sentence describes a situation where the speaker seeks help from their teacher because they couldn’t solve a problem alone. The idiom "Two heads are better than one" means that collaboration or seeking advice from someone else can lead to better solutions than working alone.

Let's Explain All IDIOMS & Their Meanings:

Two wrongs don’t make a right. – Do galatiyon se ek sahi kaam nahi hota – Just because someone did something wrong doesn’t mean you should do the same in return.
Example: "He cheated on me, but I won’t do the same because two wrongs don’t make a right."

You can’t always get what you want. – Har baar wahi nahi milta jo tum chahte ho – Life doesn’t always fulfill our desires.
Example: "I wanted the new phone, but my parents said no. Well, you can’t always get what you want."

When the going gets tough, the tough get going. – Jab mushkilen aati hain, toh mazboot log kadam badhate hain – Strong people take action when faced with difficulties.
Example: "Even though the project was challenging, she didn’t give up—when the going gets tough, the tough get going."

Two heads are better than one. – Ek se bhale do – Working together leads to better ideas or solutions.
Example: "Let’s discuss this problem together—two heads are better than one!"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Two heads are better than one." is "Collaboration leads to better solutions" because the speaker sought help from their teacher to solve a difficult problem. The other idioms do not fit the context of seeking assistance.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Copycat
(MTS Non Technical 2020)
options: One who copies all drawings of cats
One who loves cats and dogs
One who doesn’t like cats as pets
One who imitates another closely
solution:
The correct answer is: One who imitates another closely

Explanation:
"Copycat" - "नकलची" (Nakalchi)
The term "copycat" refers to someone who mimics or imitates another person's actions, behavior, or work, often without originality.

Origin of the Idiom:
The word "copycat" originated in the early 19th century, combining "copy" (to imitate) and "cat" (possibly referencing the playful or sneaky nature of cats). It is commonly used to describe someone who replicates another's work, especially in a childish or unoriginal manner.

Example:
"Stop being such a copycat and come up with your own ideas!"
"इतना नकलची बनना बंद करो और अपने खुद के विचार लेकर आओ!"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "copycat" is "One who imitates another closely" because it directly refers to mimicking behavior. The other options are unrelated and do not align with the idiom's meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Let down
(CHSL 2021 Tier I)
options: To nurse
To hire
To care about
To fail
solution:
The correct answer is: To fail

Explanation:
"Let down" - "निराश करना"
The idiom "let down" means to disappoint someone or fail to meet their expectations. It implies a sense of betrayal or unmet trust.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from the idea of lowering something (or someone) from a higher position, symbolizing a fall in expectations or support. Over time, it evolved to represent emotional disappointment.

Example:
"He promised to help, but he let me down at the last moment."
"उसने मदद करने का वादा किया था, लेकिन आखिरी समय पर उसने मुझे निराश कर दिया।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "let down" is "to fail" because it conveys the idea of disappointing someone or not fulfilling a promise. The other options ("to nurse," "to hire," "to care about") are unrelated to this idiom's meaning.

question:
Select the option that gives the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
I am working on too many projects. I think I have bitten off more than I can chew.
(CGLE 2021 Tier I)
options: To find work dull
Not able to finish work
To take on more than one can handle
To be happy to multitask
solution:
The correct answer is: To take on more than one can handle

Explanation:
"Bitten off more than one can chew" - "जितना संभाल सकें, उससे अधिक का दायित्व लेना"
The idiom means accepting more responsibilities or tasks than one can manage effectively. In the given sentence, the speaker realizes they have taken on too many projects, indicating they have overcommitted themselves.

Origin of the Idiom:
This phrase originates from the literal act of taking a bite of food that is too large to chew comfortably. Over time, it evolved into a metaphor for overcommitting or taking on excessive responsibilities.

Example:
"She agreed to organize the event, lead the team, and train the interns—now she’s realizing she’s bitten off more than she can chew."
"उसने इवेंट आयोजित करने, टीम का नेतृत्व करने और इंटर्न को ट्रेन करने की जिम्मेदारी ली—अब उसे एहसास हो रहा है कि उसने अपनी क्षमता से अधिक काम ले लिया है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "bitten off more than one can chew" is "to take on more than one can handle" because it perfectly describes the situation of overcommitting oneself. The other options do not align with the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Which of the following statements uses the given idiom correctly?
(i) When we vent our spleen we generally feel good.
(ii) Consult a doctor for controlling the damage to your system when you vent your spleen.
(iii) His latest article in the newspaper vents his spleen on bureaucracy and the prevalence of red-tapism.

(IB ACIO II Exe)
options: Only statements (ii) and (iii)
Only statements (i) and (ii)
Only statements (i) and (iii)
All the statements
solution:
The correct answer is: Only statements (i) and (iii)

Explanation:
"Vent one's spleen" - "गुस्सा निकालना / आक्रोश प्रकट करना"
This idiom means to express anger, frustration, or strong criticism. Statements (i) and (iii) correctly use the idiom to describe releasing anger (i) or criticizing something strongly (iii). Statement (ii) incorrectly interprets the idiom literally, suggesting medical advice for spleen damage, which is unrelated to the figurative meaning.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the ancient belief that the spleen was the source of emotions like anger and melancholy. "Venting" refers to releasing these pent-up emotions.

Example:
"After the meeting, she vented her spleen about the unfair policies."
"बैठक के बाद, उसने अनुचित नीतियों के बारे में अपना गुस्सा निकाला।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Only statements (i) and (iii)" is "expressing anger or frustration" because both statements use the idiom figuratively. Statement (ii) misinterprets it literally, making it incorrect. The other options do not align with the idiom's true meaning.

question:
Select the appropriate idiom that can replace the underlined phrase in the following sentence.

Geet talks incessantly about cycling in her town.
(Constable GD Examination 2022)
options: has a bee in her bonnet
put a bee on someone
makes a bee line
gives a buzz
solution:
The correct answer is: has a bee in her bonnet

Explanation:
The idiom "has a bee in her bonnet" means to be obsessed with or constantly talking about a particular idea or topic, which fits perfectly with Geet talking incessantly about cycling.

Let's Explain All IDIOMS & Their Meanings:

has a bee in her bonnet – (किसी बात का जुनून सवार होना) – To be preoccupied or obsessed with a particular idea.
Example: "She has a bee in her bonnet about starting her own business."

put a bee on someone – (किसी को परेशान करना) – (This is not a standard idiom in English.)
(Not applicable as it is not a recognized idiom.)

makes a bee line – (सीधे जाना) – To go directly and quickly toward something.
Example: "As soon as the meeting ended, he made a beeline for the exit."

gives a buzz – (फोन करना / संक्षिप्त संदेश देना) – To call someone or give a quick message.
Example: "I'll give you a buzz when I reach the station."

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "has a bee in her bonnet" is "being obsessed with a particular idea" because Geet is constantly talking about cycling, indicating an obsession. The other options do not fit the context of the sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
The actor decided to live life in the fast lane.
(MTS Non Tech Havaldar CBIC and CBN Examination 2023)
options: Racing away to the moon
A life filled with excitement
Dropping charges of crime
A life of extreme speed
solution:
The correct answer is: A life filled with excitement

Explanation:
"Live life in the fast lane" - "रोमांच से भरा जीवन जीना"
This idiom refers to living a thrilling, adventurous, or high-energy lifestyle, often involving excitement, risks, or indulgence. The phrase does not literally mean speed but rather an intense way of living.

Origin of the Idiom:
The idiom originates from highway terminology, where the "fast lane" is the lane used for overtaking or high-speed driving. Metaphorically, it represents a lifestyle that is dynamic, unrestrained, and full of activity.

Example:
"After quitting his corporate job, he started living life in the fast lane—traveling the world and taking up extreme sports."
"अपनी नौकरी छोड़ने के बाद, उसने रोमांच से भरा जीवन जीना शुरू कर दिया—दुनिया घूमना और एक्सट्रीम स्पोर्ट्स करना।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "live life in the fast lane" is "a life filled with excitement" because it conveys a high-energy, adventurous lifestyle. The other options are either literal misinterpretations or unrelated to the idiom's figurative meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.
After much of efforts, I could finally hit the nail on the head and succeed.
(Stenographer Grade C and D Examination 2023)
options: Make an error
Speak or act precisely
Accidentally injure oneself
Complete a task swiftly
solution:
The correct answer is: Speak or act precisely

Explanation:
"Hit the nail on the head" - "सही बात कहना या सटीक कार्य करना"
This idiom means to say or do something exactly right, addressing the issue perfectly. In the given sentence, the speaker succeeded after much effort because they finally acted or spoke in the most accurate way possible.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase comes from carpentry, where hitting a nail directly on its head ensures it goes in straight and does the job correctly. Over time, it evolved into a metaphor for accuracy in speech or action.

Example:
"Her explanation about the problem hit the nail on the head—now we know exactly how to fix it."
"उसकी समस्या की व्याख्या ने सही बात कही—अब हमें पता है कि इसे कैसे ठीक करना है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Hit the nail on the head" is "Speak or act precisely" because it refers to doing or saying something in the most accurate way. The other options do not align with the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.Make a beeline for
(Stenographer 2020)
options: To try and collect all the free items
To move directly towards something
To put bees in a line
To stand patiently in a queue
solution:
The correct answer is: To move directly towards something

Explanation:
"Make a beeline for" - "सीधे किसी ओर जाना"
This idiom means to head straight toward a destination or goal without any detours, much like how bees fly directly back to their hive in a straight line.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the behavior of honeybees, which are known to fly in a straight, direct path ("bee line") back to their hive after collecting nectar. This natural behavior inspired the idiom to describe swift, purposeful movement.

Example:
"As soon as the gates opened, the children made a beeline for the playground."
"जैसे ही गेट खुले, बच्चे सीधे खेल के मैदान की ओर भागे।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Make a beeline for" is "To move directly towards something" because it reflects the idiom's association with quick and purposeful movement. The other options are unrelated to the idiom's true meaning.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
To bridge the gap
(CHSL Exam 2022 Tier I)
options: To reduce differences and reconcile
To push people apart
To slander someone
To mend a broken bridge
solution:
The correct answer is: To reduce differences and reconcile

Explanation:
"To bridge the gap" - "अंतर को कम करना और सुलह करना"
This idiom means to reduce differences between two opposing sides or to bring people closer by resolving conflicts. The correct option fits best because it directly conveys the idea of closing a divide, whether in opinions, relationships, or understanding.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from the literal act of building a bridge to connect two separated land masses, symbolizing the effort to bring together disconnected or conflicting parties.

Example:
"The mediator helped bridge the gap between the two arguing teams."
"मध्यस्थ ने दो झगड़ते दलों के बीच अंतर को कम करने में मदद की।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "To bridge the gap" is "To reduce differences and reconcile" because it signifies efforts to bring harmony or understanding between conflicting sides. The other options either imply division ("To push people apart"), defamation ("To slander someone"), or a literal interpretation ("To mend a broken bridge"), which do not match the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.Pick and choose
(MTS Non Technical 2020)
options: Select only the best from choices
Start a quarrel or a fight over something
Start all over again after a crisis
Question someone on a topic
solution:
The correct answer is: Select only the best from choices

Explanation:
"Pick and choose" - "सर्वोत्तम का चयन करना"
This idiom means to carefully select only the best or most suitable options from a range of choices, often implying a selective or discerning approach.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from the literal act of picking (selecting) and choosing (deciding) the best items, such as fruits or goods, from a larger group. Over time, it evolved into a figurative expression for careful selection.

Example:
"She didn’t just accept any job offer; she took her time to pick and choose the best one."
"उसने कोई भी नौकरी का प्रस्ताव स्वीकार नहीं किया; उसने सर्वोत्तम का चयन करने के लिए समय लिया।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Pick and choose" is "Select only the best from choices" because it emphasizes a deliberate and selective approach. The other options do not align with the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom below.
“The grass is greener on the other side”

(Constable Driver and DCPO Group C)
options: Get organized and do things effectively
if you sort out a problem immediately it may save a lot of extra work later.
something that you say that means that other people always seem to be in a better situation than you, although they may not be
to have very serious problems that limit the ways in which you can act
solution:
The correct answer is: something that you say that means that other people always seem to be in a better situation than you, although they may not be

Explanation:
"The grass is greener on the other side" - "दूसरों की स्थिति हमेशा बेहतर लगती है"
This idiom expresses the idea that people often believe others are in a more favorable position than themselves, even when that may not be true. It highlights human tendency to envy what others have while overlooking their own advantages.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from the observation that grass appears more lush and green from a distance. Farmers or herdsmen may have noticed that pastures beyond their own fences seemed more fertile, symbolizing the illusion that others' lives are better.

Example:
"She always complains about her job, thinking that her friends have better careers, but the grass is greener on the other side."
"वह हमेशा अपनी नौकरी की शिकायत करती है, यह सोचकर कि उसके दोस्तों के पास बेहतर करियर है, लेकिन दूसरों की स्थिति हमेशा बेहतर लगती है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "The grass is greener on the other side" is "others' situations always seem better, though they may not be" because it captures the essence of perceived superiority in others' circumstances. The other options are unrelated to this idiom's meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Separate the wheat from the chaff
(Stenographer Grade C and D Examination 2022)
options: To separate the valuable from the worthless
Harvesting crops and cooking them
Farming barren lands with little water
Cooking food during famine
solution:
The correct answer is: To separate the valuable from the worthless

Explanation:
"Separate the wheat from the chaff" - "अच्छे को बुरे से अलग करना"
This idiom means to distinguish valuable or useful things from worthless ones. Wheat (valuable grain) is separated from chaff (worthless husk) during threshing, making this the most fitting meaning.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from agriculture, where farmers separate edible wheat grains from inedible chaff by winnowing or threshing. Over time, it evolved metaphorically to describe filtering out what is essential from what is not.

Example:
"The interview process helps separate the wheat from the chaff by identifying the best candidates."
"साक्षात्कार प्रक्रिया सर्वश्रेष्ठ उम्मीदवारों की पहचान करके अच्छे को बुरे से अलग करने में मदद करती है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Separate the wheat from the chaff" is "To separate the valuable from the worthless" because it aligns with the idiom’s agricultural and metaphorical sense of distinguishing quality. The other options are unrelated or literal misinterpretations.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.
An ox on their tongue was the only way officers would have allowed him to carry on the unlawful activities he was involved in.

(Constable GD Examination 2022)
options: Bribed to remain silent
Getting no appreciation
Being frank
Telling lies
solution:
The correct answer is: Bribed to remain silent

Explanation:
"An ox on their tongue" - "चुप रहने के लिए रिश्वत देना"
This idiom implies that someone has been bribed to stay silent or not reveal the truth. In the given sentence, the officers were likely bribed ("an ox on their tongue") to ignore unlawful activities.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from ancient practices where an ox (a valuable asset) was used as a bribe to ensure someone's silence or cooperation. It symbolizes a heavy payment to suppress the truth.

Example:
"The corrupt official had an ox on his tongue, so he never reported the illegal mining."
"भ्रष्ट अधिकारी के मुँह में बैल था, इसलिए उसने अवैध खनन की शिकायत नहीं की।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Bribed to remain silent" is "चुप रहने के लिए रिश्वत देना" because it directly relates to silencing someone through bribery. The other options do not fit the context of the idiom.
